name: Lavender oil capsules (Silexan)

lead: Silexan is a capsule containing a standardized lavender oil, taken for anxiety and restlessness.
Controlled trials report reduced anxiety, though the NCCIH says oral effectiveness is not established. It has no studied appearance use.

paras: Linalool and linalyl acetate are the main constituents. How the oral product acts is not settled in the sources reviewed.
Pure lavender oil is toxic if swallowed in quantity, with poisonings reported mostly in children. Topical oil can cause contact dermatitis, and interactions with some drugs have been noted.

label.generic: ADVANCED CARE LAVENDER FRESH DRY SPRAY 48H ANTIPERSPIRANT DEODORANT

lead: Silexan is a standardized oral lavender oil preparation sold as capsules for anxiety and restlessness. It is made from Lavandula angustifolia flowers and marketed in Germany as a medicine and in the US as a supplement (CalmAid), according to a reference page.[1]

Placebo-controlled trials of a daily oral dose reported reduced anxiety symptoms, and a 2010 trial compared it with lorazepam. The NCCIH states that the effectiveness of oral lavender for anxiety is not established.[1] Lavender oil is also used in aromatherapy, perfumery and cosmetics, where its constituents include linalool and linalyl acetate.[1][2]
Silexan has no studied appearance use. It is a recovery-category compound for anxiety and sleep. Lavender oil is toxic if swallowed in large amounts, especially for children.[1]
infobox: Standardized oral lavender oil (Silexan; Lasea in Germany; CalmAid in the US)
Medicine for anxiety restlessness in Germany; GRAS listing for lavender oil in US

paras: Lavender oil is distilled from flower spikes and is among the most commonly adulterated essential oils, according to a reference page.[1] Reviews of its biological activities describe antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory laboratory findings alongside traditional calming uses.[2][3] Silexan is a specific, standardized oral product distinct from topical or aromatherapy oils.

A 2010 trial reported effects comparable to lorazepam in generalized anxiety disorder, and a 2024 patient-level analysis of placebo-controlled trials reported reduced anxiety symptoms at 80 mg daily versus placebo.[1] The NCCIH states that aromatherapy and topical lavender have no established clinical benefit and that oral effectiveness for anxiety is undetermined; a 2022 guideline suggested it may be useful in depression.[1]

The FDA lists lavender oil as generally recognized as safe for its intended uses. Swallowing about 5 mL of diluted essential oil may cause toxicity in adults and 2 to 3 mL in children, and New South Wales recorded 271 reported poisonings in 2014 to 2018, mostly in children. Topical use can cause contact dermatitis, and ingestion may interact with anticoagulants, statins and anticonvulsants. Lavender oil is described as a potential endocrine disruptor.[1]
No community discussion of Silexan was found for this entry.

Controlled trials of oral Silexan in anxiety are summarised above.[1] Separate registered trials of inhaled lavender aromatherapy test anxiety and pain around medical procedures, in dental settings and in hemodialysis.[4][5][6] A study in a dental office found ambient lavender and orange odors reduced anxiety and improved mood.[7] These involve inhalation, not oral Silexan. No studies of oral lavender for appearance were found.
